composition: Nominal composition Fe–28Mn–9Al–0.9C (all in weight percent), i.e. the Ni-free grade of the Fe-Mn-Al-C-(Ni) family; Ni is deliberately absent (reported as "–"). Wet chemical analysis / emission spectroscopy gives Mn 28.3 ± 0.4 wt.%, Al 9.0 ± 0.05 wt.%, C 0.9 ± 0.01 wt.%, Fe balance. The design intent is a high-Mn, high-Al, ~0.9C austenitic low-density steel: Mn and C stabilize the austenite at room temperature, while Al lowers the physical density and is a ferrite stabilizer that also promotes intermetallic (B2/κ-carbide) formation. Because this alloy carries no Ni, it cannot form the Ni-rich ordered B2 precipitates that control recrystallization in the two Ni-bearing sibling alloys (28Mn5Ni and 15Mn5Ni), and it therefore serves as the baseline for isolating the effect of Ni addition.
conclusions: For the Ni-free 28Mn0Ni alloy the 1023 K/1 h treatment sits at the transition where the cold-rolled austenite is essentially fully recrystallized (fraction 0.8–1.0) with fine equiaxed grains and low stored strain, yet still a low fraction of fine B2 particles. The resulting property set (YS 732 ± 2 MPa, UTS 1051 ± 5 MPa, TE 36 ± 2%, n = 0.30) is a compromise: it loses much of the strength achieved by annealing at 973 K (YS ~900 MPa, TE ~23%) but gains substantial ductility, and it is far weaker and more ductile than the Ni-bearing siblings at the same condition (28Mn5Ni: 1289 ± 2 MPa YS, 1537 ± 2 MPa UTS, 17 ± 1% TE; 15Mn5Ni: brittle with <1% elongation). Ductile dimple rupture confirms the ductile failure mode at 1023 K for this alloy, in contrast to the crack-initiation-controlled quasi-cleavage intergranular fracture of 15Mn5Ni. The results show that Ni addition is what delays recrystallization and widens the two-phase processing window, whereas the Ni-free alloy has the fastest recrystallization/grain-coarsening kinetics and the highest strain-hardening exponent. Practically, the optimal processing temperature window for 28Mn0Ni is identified as ~973 K (fine tuning temperature/time around it), since a 50 K increase accelerates recrystallization at the expense of a drastic strength reduction; the study thus establishes the composition–recrystallization–precipitation coupling that governs strength–ductility optimization in austenitic low-density steels processed in the two-phase region.
mechanisms: Recrystallization vs. precipitation competition: at 1023 K the cold-rolled 28Mn0Ni austenite recrystallizes almost completely (fraction 0.8–1.0), whereas the Ni-bearing alloys remain largely unrecrystallized; because this alloy is nearly B2-free, no concurrent fine-precipitate drag retards boundary migration, so its recrystallization and grain-growth kinetics are far faster than in the Ni-containing grades.

Nucleation sites: recrystallized grains nucleate predominantly along γ/γ boundaries and γ/B2 interfaces; the sparse intragranular B2 particles do not pin new recrystallized grains but may delay the overall recovery process.

Successive 50 K temperature increase (973 K → 1023 K) accelerates recrystallization kinetics sharply but at the cost of strength: the microstructure moves from a bimodal partly-deformed/partly-recrystallized state (YS ~900 MPa, 23% elongation) to a fully recrystallized one (YS 732 MPa, 36% elongation).

Strain hardening in fully recrystallized austenite proceeds by planar slip activity followed by dynamic slip band refinement, with dislocation–twin interaction involving prior annealing twins acting as an additional strain-hardening mechanism in the recrystallized alloys.

Fine κ-carbides and B2 particles promote glide-plane softening, which contributes to a higher strain-hardening rate; conversely a high fraction of coarse κ-carbide-bearing deformed austenite (as at 973 K) limits strain hardening and ductility.

Absence of Ni is responsible for the high strain-hardening capability of this alloy: after the same 1173 K treatment n rises to 0.50 for 28Mn0Ni versus ~0.30 for both Ni-bearing alloys, because the alloy has no non-shearable Ni-rich B2 particles to cause inhomogeneous slip-band spacing and early slip-band refinement.

The heat-treatment temperature window is bounded by κ-carbide dissolution: only below the κ-carbide dissolution temperature does the deformed, κ-carbide-bearing zone provide strengthening, so the useful processing window for 28Mn0Ni is around 973 K, and moving 50 K above it collapses the strength–ductility balance.
microstructure: In the HR+CR+1023 K condition the microstructure consists of a nearly single-phase austenitic (FCC) matrix with a low fraction of fine secondary B2 particles (two phases in total). The OIM-EBSD phase map is essentially uniform red (FCC) with only sparse, fine blue (B2) particles dispersed within the grains. Annealing at 1023 K drives the cold-rolled structure to essentially complete recrystallization — the recrystallized fraction of austenite at ~1023 K lies between 0.8 and 1.0 — producing fine, equiaxed, randomly oriented recrystallized austenite grains (multiply coloured IPF map, nearly random texture). Consistent with this, the kernel average misorientation (KAM) map is almost uniformly dark blue (near-minimum misorientation, i.e. low stored strain / low local misorientation), with only a few isolated green or yellow-green spots. The residual second phase is B2, an ordered BCC, FeAl-based intermetallic; in the general heat-treated condition two B2 morphologies are distinguished — fine intragranular B2 of 50–200 nm and coarser intergranular B2 of 0.5–1.5 μm (the former not indexable by SEM-EBSD). The γ/B2 interface is the relevant phase boundary; in this Ni-free alloy the intragranular B2 particles are inferred not to pin the newly recrystallized grains but to delay overall recovery, and nucleation of recrystallized grains occurs mainly along γ/γ boundaries and γ/B2 interfaces. For the 28Mn0Ni alloy the cold-rolled structure progresses from partial recrystallization at 973 K to complete recrystallization at 1023 K, followed by significant grain growth at 1173 K.
processing: The alloy was prepared by vacuum induction melting to a 30 kg ingot. The sound portion was homogenized at 1423 K for 2.5 h and then hot rolled at 1323 K to a final plate thickness of about 13 mm (this condition is denoted HR). Samples cut from the hot-rolled plate were cold rolled at room temperature in several passes to ~50% reduction in thickness (~6 mm sheets), denoted HR+CR; 50% was chosen as the common reduction for all three alloys because the 15Mn5Ni counterpart cracked beyond that level. The cold-rolled sheets were then heat treated at 1023 K for 1 h followed by water quenching; the sample is named after this heat-treatment temperature (HR+CR+1023 K). 1023 K lies inside the two-phase (austenite + secondary phase) processing window, i.e. above the 973 K condition where recrystallization is only partial and below the 1173 K condition where the austenite is fully recrystallized, coarsened and precipitate-free.
properties: Room-temperature tensile properties (measured on ASTM E8M flat specimens, gauge length 30 mm, width 6 mm, thickness 4–5 mm, constant cross-head speed 0.5 mm min⁻¹ corresponding to an initial strain rate of ~3 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; tests triplicated and averaged): yield stress (0.2% offset) 732 ± 2 MPa, ultimate tensile strength 1051 ± 5 MPa, total tensile elongation to failure 36 ± 2%, and strain-hardening exponent n = 0.30. Fractography of the 1023 K tensile specimen shows ductile dimple rupture, in contrast to the brittle (<1% elongation) behaviour of the 15Mn5Ni alloy under the same condition. No Vickers hardness value is reported explicitly for 28Mn0Ni at 1023 K (hardness was plotted only at 873, 973, 1073, 1173 and 1273 K, decreasing monotonically with temperature). Key characterization techniques applied to this sample: OIM-EBSD (Zeiss Supra 55 FEG-SEM with Oxford Nordley EBSD and EDS detectors; step size 120 nm on ~100×100 μm² areas; coloured IPF, phase-contrast and KAM maps analysed with TSL-OIM software, with GOS < 2° criterion and KAM used to quantify recrystallization) and room-temperature tensile testing. XRD and TEM for this alloy were reported only at 973 K and 1173 K, not at 1023 K.
summary: Ni-free austenitic low-density steel Fe–28Mn–9Al–0.9C (designated 28Mn0Ni) in the hot-rolled + 50% cold-rolled + 1023 K/1 h water-quenched condition. It is the Ni-free reference alloy of a study that used thermo-mechanical processing in the two-phase (γ + secondary phase) region to trade off concurrent κ-carbide/B2 precipitation against recrystallization of the cold-rolled austenite. At 1023 K the alloy reaches essentially complete recrystallization (fraction 0.8–1.0) and yields an intermediate strength–ductility balance (YS 732 ± 2 MPa, UTS 1051 ± 5 MPa, TE 36 ± 2%).
unmapped: The fraction of recrystallized austenite at the ~1023 K intermediate data point of 28Mn0Ni lies between 0.8 and 1.0 (Fig. 5a) — a range, not a single value.

XRD patterns for 28Mn0Ni are reported only for HR+CR, HR+CR+973 K and HR+CR+1173 K: κ-carbide and B2 peaks appear at 973 K and only γ peaks remain at 1173 K; no XRD trace exists for the 1023 K condition, so the phase constitution at 1023 K is inferred rather than directly diffracted.

TEM analysis for 28Mn0Ni was performed at 973 K (mixed recrystallized/deformed austenite with intragranular κ-carbides 10–60 nm and intergranular B2) and at 1173 K (precipitate-free); no TEM data specific to the 1023 K condition is provided.

No explicit Vickers hardness data point is reported for 28Mn0Ni at 1023 K; Fig. 8b plots hardness only at 873, 973, 1073, 1173 and 1273 K, and for 28Mn0Ni hardness decreases monotonically with heat-treatment temperature (falling below 200 VHN at 1273 K).

Twin fraction quantification: for 28Mn0Ni the twin fraction rises from just below 0.1 at 973 K to just under 0.6 at 1173 K (Fig. 5c); by 1023 K it is on the rising trend but an exact value at 1023 K is not tabulated.

Post-tensile interrupted-deformation TEM for 28Mn0Ni is reported for the HR+CR+973 K (dislocation multiplication and cell formation, ε~0.14) and HR+CR+1173 K (planar slip → slip-band refinement → dislocation–annealing-twin interaction at ε~0.02/0.08/0.30) conditions, not for 1023 K.

Hardness of cold-rolled 28Mn0Ni saturates near ~450 VHN at 50% reduction, with the initial HR hardness around 256 ± 5 VHN and a lower initial work-hardening rate than the Ni-containing alloys followed by a more rapid rise at higher reductions.
